chunks.rationale: electron/services.js removeProject is the whole bug. The old code threw THREAD_STILL_HAS_WORKTREE if ANY thread in the project still had a worktreePath — on the live store that is 150/413 threads for solenta (148 of them archived), 24/48 AppVideo, 29/59 huskyscout, 12/14 Shipnest-v2, so every project was unremovable. Read the active-run guard first (unchanged, still runs over every thread before anything is deleted), then the new teardown loop: git worktree remove --force, git branch -D per thread, one git worktree prune, all via lazily-required gitTry so no require cycle with worktrees.js. Failures are deliberately ignored — gitTry catches execFileSync throws (including ENOENT on a missing cwd) and returns {ok:false}, which is what makes a deleted dir / gone branch / gone checkout non-blocking. cleanupWorktree was deliberately NOT reused: it does store.updateThread + store.save() per thread, and the live store is 143 MB, so 150 threads would mean 150 full-file rewrites.
risks: --force discards uncommitted work in those worktrees. That is why the Sidebar confirm now names the count; the guard used to be the protection and is gone.

Removing a project deletes the worktrees of ALL its threads, including the one you are reading this in if it belongs to that project. The active-run guard only covers threads that are currently running.

Teardown runs before the purge, so a thread row still exists while its worktree is deleted. If the process dies mid-loop, some worktrees are gone but the project remains — recoverable (rerun Remove), unlike the reverse order.

150 sequential sync git spawns block the main process for a few seconds on the solenta project. Acceptable for a one-shot destructive action; do not make it async without re-checking the active-run guard's read of thread.status.

chunks.rationale: electron/test/remove-project.test.js: the two tests that asserted the OLD guard are rewritten — removeProject now SUCCEEDS with a worktree present, and the shared-string test keeps asserting deleteThread's guard only (THREAD_STILL_HAS_WORKTREE is still exported and still used there). The new cases build a real repo + real git worktree add and assert the dir and branch are actually gone afterwards, plus a stale-path case where worktreePath points at a directory that no longer exists. test/appWiring.test.tsx pins that a rejected projects.remove puts the real reason on [data-toast=error]; test/sidebar.test.tsx pins the worktree copy (plural, singular, and absent when no thread has a path).
risks: The teardown tests shell out to real git. They pass here; a sandbox without git on PATH would fail them differently from the rest of the suite.

npm run test:electron needs node_modules, core/node_modules, core/dist and memory-server/node_modules symlinked from the main checkout or it reports hundreds of unrelated MODULE_NOT_FOUND failures — that is what the worker first mistook for regressions.

chunks.rationale: Renderer half. src/App.tsx handleRemoveProject no longer swallows the error: catch reads err.message and stores 'Failed to remove "slug": <reason>' (prefix alone when the message is empty) in removeFailMessage — renamed from removeFailSlug because it now holds a full sentence — and still rethrows so the Sidebar confirm closes. The existing ArchiveToast error variant is reused. src/components/Sidebar.tsx counts threads in that project with a worktreePath and, when non-zero, adds 'Deletes N worktree(s) from disk, including any uncommitted changes in them.'; the now-false 'This removes only this project entry.' becomes 'The repository checkout itself is not deleted.'
risks: A main-process message that itself started with 'Failed to remove' would double-prefix. Neither current reason does.
Long git stderr would render as one long toast line; there is no truncation and no body slot on ArchiveToast.

The count comes from live ThreadInfo.worktreePath, not a disk scan: pendingWorktree threads are excluded (nothing on disk yet) and stale paths still count (harmless — the backend force-removes and tolerates failure).

Not verified in a live Electron window. Doing so means actually removing a real project and deleting its worktrees off disk, which is destructive on this machine — left for Willem to trigger deliberately.

Verified on the merged tree, not just per worker: node --test electron/test/remove-project.test.js 10/10; npm run test:renderer 1335/1335; npm run typecheck clean; npm run test:electron 1644/1645 on the first run and 1645/1645 on a rerun (the one failure is the known flaky web-integration reconnect test, not this change).
Solenta's ~96 GB of worktrees are still only reclaimed by removing a project or by worktreeRetention, which remains unset on every project (separate concern, not touched here).
